passage: At 11:40 on a Sunday night, Gautam's history essay on the salt march had exactly one paragraph. His classmate Kishore had messaged an hour earlier: "Just paste the question into the chatbot, bro. Takes two minutes. Ma'am never checks." Gautam opened the chatbot tab, typed half the prompt, and stopped. Last month Mrs. Rao had read out his essay on the Partition trains, the one with his Dadi's story in it, and the whole class had gone quiet. Nobody else could have written that one. He deleted the prompt. He pulled out his notes, messy blue ink and arrows everywhere, and wrote until 1:15. The middle section came out clumsy. On Monday Kishore grinned and said, "Full marks, easy." Gautam shrugged, tired but strangely light, and handed in his own four pages.

qa.q: What time did Gautam finish writing his essay?
qa.a: He wrote until 1:15 on Sunday night.

qa.q: Why did Gautam stop halfway through typing the prompt?
qa.a: He remembered feeling proud when the class went quiet over his Partition essay with his Dadi's story, and he felt uneasy about handing in words that were not his.

qa.q: What small step helped Gautam get started on his own?
qa.a: He pulled out his handwritten notes instead of staring at a blank page, so the essay could grow from material he already had.

qa.q: How might Kishore see Gautam's choice?
qa.a: Kishore probably thinks Gautam wasted a night on something a chatbot could do in two minutes, and may not understand why owning the work mattered to him.

grounding: Shows a teen turning down an AI-written shortcut and choosing to hand in work that is truly his own.

passage: I'm Leela, and I sat two benches behind Neelam the whole term, so I saw most of it. When Sir asked who would run the science-fair stall, nobody moved, and Neelam put her hand up. She drew a chart on the back of a notebook: who builds the water-filter model, who writes the poster, who explains it to visitors. She messaged the group every evening, not bossy, just "Anyone stuck?" On the day, the filter leaked all over the table and the judges frowned. I expected her to blame the boy who had sealed the joints. Instead she said, "I told him to rush it. That's on me." Her voice shook a little, I think. Afterward she asked each of us what she should do differently next time. I don't know what she felt inside, but I'd work with her again.

qa.q: What did the group build for the science-fair stall?
qa.a: They built a water-filter model.

qa.q: What does Neelam's shaking voice suggest about how she felt when she took the blame?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous and embarrassed about the failure, yet determined to own it instead of blaming a teammate, though Leela admits not knowing for sure.

qa.q: What could Neelam try next time to avoid a last-minute leak?
qa.a: She could plan a test run a day early, so the group has time to fix problems instead of rushing the joints.

qa.q: What is it like for the boy who sealed the joints when Neelam says it is on her?
qa.a: He is spared being shamed in front of the judges, so he probably feels relieved and may trust her more as a leader.

grounding: Shows a student taking charge of a group project, keeping peers going, and accepting the blame when it fails.

passage: Sarika's phone buzzed with the group chat, all lowercase slang and memes, while her mother called from the kitchen in Assamese: "Sarika, pitha khabi?" Two classmates sat at the dining table colouring a geography map, and one of them, Bhupen, looked up. Last year Sarika would have answered in quick Hindi and pretended not to hear the rest. Her cheeks still warmed a little. This time she called back in Assamese, then turned to the table. "She's asking if we want pitha. Rice cakes. My grandmother's recipe." Bhupen said, "Wait, say that again?" and tried the word, badly. Sarika laughed and corrected him, twice. Later she typed in the chat, "ok the pitha was elite," and switched back to English for the map legend without thinking twice about any of it.

qa.q: What were Sarika and her classmates working on at the dining table?
qa.a: They were colouring a geography map.

qa.q: How can you tell Sarika still felt a little self-conscious about speaking Assamese in front of classmates?
qa.a: Her cheeks warmed and she remembered hiding it in Hindi last year, so some embarrassment was still there, but pride won and she answered in Assamese anyway.

qa.q: What made the moment go well, and what could Sarika keep doing?
qa.a: She explained the word simply and let Bhupen try it, turning her home language into something to share; she can keep switching languages openly instead of hiding one.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see Sarika's home language?
qa.a: He seems curious rather than mocking, since he asks her to repeat the word and tries to say it himself 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teen moving between home, school and online language easily and showing pride in her heritage.

passage:
Monday: At the bus stop, Vidya's friend grumbled that "people from outside" were crowding the city. Vidya nodded, not really thinking about it.
Thursday: For a social-science project on migration, she sat on the building steps with Gautam, the night watchman, and asked why he had left his village in Bihar. He talked about a flooded field, two younger sisters still in school, and his first winter sleeping on a relative's floor. She wrote until her pen ran dry, then asked what he missed most. "My mother's voice in the morning," he said.
The next Tuesday: She presented his story, with his permission, beside a map showing how people have always moved for work. At the bus stop that evening, the same grumble came. Vidya asked, "Do you know anyone who actually moved here?" Her friend went quiet, then said, "My own grandfather, actually."

qa.q: Where did Gautam live before he came to the city?
qa.a: He left his village in Bihar.

qa.q: What does Vidya's question at the bus stop suggest about how her thinking changed?
qa.a: She now feels curious and a little uncomfortable with the easy grumble, and wants her friend to picture real people like Gautam instead of faceless outsiders.

qa.q: Which choice helped Vidya understand migration better, and why?
qa.a: Sitting down to listen to Gautam and asking open questions, like what he missed, turned a vague idea into one person's real reasons and feelings.

qa.q: What might it mean to Gautam that a student asked about his story?
qa.a: He might feel respected and seen, since he shared personal memories and agreed to let her present them.

grounding: Shows a teen's curiosity about a migrant's story softening a prejudiced remark over several days.

subtype: Handling Failure, Result Disappointment & Family Crisis
passage: You want the honest version, Mohit? Okay. The week the prelim results came, I got 52 in maths. Same week, Appa's shop shut down, and every night I could hear him and Amma arguing through the wall about the rent. I stopped eating breakfast. My aunt kept saying, "Keerthana, results aren't everything," which didn't help at all. What helped was small stuff. Our class teacher sat with me after the result and circled the three chapters where I lost most marks. She also asked, quietly, if things were okay at home, and I actually told her. She said she'd call Amma, and she did, that same evening. I made a timetable with just those three chapters. Some nights I cried first and studied after. The boards are in March. I'm not okay every day, but I'm not giving up either.

qa.q: What mark did Keerthana get in maths in the prelims?
qa.a: Keerthana got 52 in maths.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling during the week of the results and the shop closing?
qa.a: Keerthana felt overwhelmed and sad, skipping breakfast and crying some nights, yet stayed hopeful enough to keep following a plan.

qa.q: How did the class teacher support Keerthana, and why did it work?
qa.a: The teacher narrowed the problem to three chapters, asked about home and called Amma the same evening, so Keerthana had a clear next step and was not carrying everything alone.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Mohit might feel moved and a little worried for Keerthana, but relieved that there is a plan and an adult helping.

grounding: Illustrates a teen coping with poor results, parental arguments and a family money crisis without losing hope.

passage:
Tuesday, first week: Thomas read the same biology paragraph four times and still couldn't say what it meant. The ceiling fan clicked, someone tapped a pen, and the words kept sliding away. He shut the book, furious with himself.
Saturday, second week: His friend Mridul quizzed him out loud while they walked to tuition, and Thomas remembered almost everything. "You're not slow," Mridul said. "You just learn by talking." That night Thomas tried reading aloud at home with earplugs in, and it worked better.
Monday, third week: Heart thumping, he stayed back after class and told Ms. Pereira that noise made reading hard and that he remembered more when he explained things aloud. She moved his seat near the window, away from the fan, and suggested he record short voice summaries. He walked out feeling lighter than he had in weeks.

qa.q: Where did Ms. Pereira move Thomas's seat?
qa.a: She moved his seat near the window, away from the fan.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when he stayed back to talk to Ms. Pereira, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was nervous, shown by his thumping heart, and afterward relieved, walking out lighter than he had felt in weeks 😰

qa.q: What could another student learn from how Thomas found his way of studying?
qa.a: Notice when learning works better, as Thomas did on the walk with Mridul, test it at home, then tell a teacher exactly what helps.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Thomas's struggle?
qa.a: Mridul doesn't see a slow student; he sees a friend who learns by talking, and tells him so plainly.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising how noise and talking affect his learning and asking a teacher for support.

passage: The pond behind the Shiv temple in Gargi's village had shrunk to a cracked brown circle by April. Her grandfather said it never used to dry before the monsoon. In science class that week, Gargi learned how burning coal and diesel traps heat, and how hotter summers pull water out of ponds and soil faster. She walked home with Yusuf, whose father ran the diesel pump for the fields. "So we stop the pump?" Yusuf asked, half joking. "No," Gargi said. "But we can do something small that's real." They went to their teacher, and the eco club set up a rooftop rain barrel at school, then a sign-up sheet for households wanting help with their own. Only six families signed up. Gargi pinned the list on the panchayat notice board anyway.

qa.q: What did the eco club set up at the school?
qa.a: The eco club set up a rooftop rain barrel.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt when only six families signed up?
qa.a: She was probably disappointed, yet still determined, since she pinned the list on the panchayat notice board anyway.

qa.q: Why was Gargi's answer to Yusuf a wise one?
qa.a: Instead of an impossible fix like stopping the pump, she chose a small, practical step the school and some families could actually take.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel about the talk of diesel and heat, given his father's job?
qa.a: Yusuf might feel a bit defensive or uneasy, which may be why he half-joked about stopping the pump.

grounding: Shows a teen linking the causes of warming to her village's drying pond and choosing a realistic group action.

passage: Farida's alarm went off at 6:10, and for the third morning in a row she wanted to switch it off. Two weeks ago she had started running laps in the colony park with her neighbour Siddharth, who was training for the school relay. The first day she had tried to keep up with him and ended up bent over near the swings, gasping. Now she ran at her own pace, walked when she needed to, and ticked off mornings on a calendar taped to her cupboard. Her mother had started keeping boiled chana and a banana on the counter, so Farida stopped grabbing chips on the way to the bus. This morning a drizzle was falling. Siddharth texted, "Still on? 🙂" She laced her shoes, grumbling under her breath, and went.

qa.q: Where did Farida run with Siddharth?
qa.a: She ran laps in the colony park.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when her alarm rang, and what made her go anyway?
qa.a: She felt reluctant and sleepy, but the ticked-off calendar and Siddharth's text helped her feel committed enough to go.

qa.q: What went wrong on the first day, and what fixed it?
qa.a: She tried to match a relay runner and ended up gasping; running at her own pace and walking when needed made the habit one she could keep.

qa.q: How might Farida's mother see her part in the new routine?
qa.a: She is likely quietly pleased that keeping easy food on the counter helps Farida eat better without any nagging.

grounding: Shows a teen building a consistent exercise and eating routine through small, repeatable steps.

passage: Sit, Shalini. You asked why I never laugh at your debate club. When I was about your age, in our small school in Madurai, a teacher, Mr. Joseph, ran a Saturday circle. Each week one of us had to explain a belief that wasn't our own: the middle path of the Buddhists, Jain non-violence, the duty taught in the Gita, even an atheist's argument from a thin library book. I, Usha, a temple priest's granddaughter, got the atheist. I was furious. I thought it was a trap. But I read it, found one point I could not answer, and said so in front of everyone. Mr. Joseph only nodded and asked, "Now which of your own beliefs will you test the same way?" I went home and argued with my father till midnight, respectfully. I still go to the temple, kanna. I just know why now.

qa.q: Which belief was Usha given to explain in the Saturday circle?
qa.a: Usha got the atheist's argument from a thin library book.

qa.q: What did Usha feel when she was given the atheist's view, and how did that change?
qa.a: Usha was furious and suspicious at first, thinking it was a trap, but after reading honestly Usha felt humbled enough to admit a point she could not answer.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned the exercise into real learning?
qa.a: Usha chose to admit in front of everyone that she couldn't answer one point, instead of pretending, and then to test her own beliefs the same way.

qa.q: How might Mr. Joseph have seen Usha's honest admission?
qa.a: Mr. Joseph was probably pleased that the circle was working, since he answered with a deeper question rather than praise or a verdict.

grounding: An elder recalls learning as a teen to compare religions and worldviews fairly, including the elder's own.

passage: So, Manjula, you asked how the solar-lamp project took seven months. Honestly? Month one was exciting. By month three, soldering the same circuit for the fifth time was boring, and I stopped opening the box. My sister called it "Chinmay's shoebox of shame." What got me back was simple. I wrote each small task on a slip of paper, like "fix the loose switch" or "test the battery for one night," and did one slip after dinner, even on days I didn't feel like it. Some slips took ten minutes. Then in month five the panel cracked, and I nearly quit for real. I sulked for a week, then saved up and ordered another one. The lamp works now. It's ugly, but I finished it, and that feels different from anything I've made before.

qa.q: How long did the solar-lamp project take?
qa.a: The project took seven months.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel when the panel cracked in month five?
qa.a: Chinmay felt discouraged enough to nearly quit and sulked for a week, before deciding to order another panel.

qa.q: What trick helped Chinmay keep going through the boring middle?
qa.a: Writing small tasks on slips and doing one after dinner each day kept progress moving without waiting to feel motivated.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's sister see the finished lamp after joking about the shoebox of shame?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a little impressed that the box she teased about became a working lamp 😊

grounding: Shows a teen sustaining a months-long project through boredom and a setback.
